blocks.text: Apple’s original iPhone software centered a finger-driven Multi-Touch interface instead of a fixed hardware keyboard. It combined calling, Visual Voicemail, SMS, calendar and contact synchronization, a camera and photo library, and widescreen music and video playback with Cover Flow.

blocks.text: Its internet layer included rich HTML Mail, Safari over Wi-Fi or EDGE, Google Maps, a dedicated YouTube client, and access to third-party services through standards-based web applications rather than native third-party installation. Apple’s retail announcement fixes the US public launch to June 29, 2007.

citations.locator: Internet communications and advanced sensors sections

blocks.text: Apple’s first iPhone update focused on web-content security. It corrected cross-site access through redirected windows, unsafe regular-expression processing, injected XMLHttpRequest headers, deceptive internationalized domain names, and memory corruption while rendering framesets.

Apple distributed the package only through iTunes and identified the resulting version as 1.0.1. Its historical security index dates the release to July 31, 2007; no broader consumer feature list survives in Apple’s bulletin.
A contemporaneous MacRumors report records Apple releasing iPhone update 1.0.2 through iTunes on August 21, 2007. The update’s published description was limited to bug fixes, with no itemized list.
Because Apple’s surviving 2007 security chronology jumps from 1.0.1 to 1.1.1, this article does not infer a security advisory or convert early user observations into confirmed changes.

events.summary: The first public iPhone software release combined phone, widescreen media, and desktop-style internet functions behind a Multi-Touch interface, establishing the application model and interaction patterns that began Apple’s mobile software history.

changes.title: Multi-Touch software interface
changes.canonicalSummary: The first release introduced a finger-operated Multi-Touch interface built around tapping, flicking, pinching, and context-specific software controls.
changes.summary: Apple treated the large touch display and software-defined controls as the common interaction layer across phone, media, and internet applications.

changes.title: Integrated calling and contacts
changes.canonicalSummary: The software connected contact lists, favorites, call history, and multi-party calling in one touch-driven Phone application.
changes.summary: Contacts could synchronize from a computer or supported internet service, while favorites and conference-call controls shortened common calling workflows.

changes.title: Visual Voicemail
changes.canonicalSummary: Visual Voicemail presented messages as a selectable list so callers could choose playback order without traversing earlier messages.
changes.summary: The feature depended on participating carrier support and was introduced as part of the original Phone experience.

changes.title: SMS and predictive software keyboard
changes.canonicalSummary: The release paired threaded SMS sessions with a full on-screen QWERTY keyboard that predicted and corrected typing.
changes.summary: The keyboard appeared when needed instead of occupying permanent hardware space, establishing a reusable text-entry surface across applications.

changes.title: Calendar and personal-data synchronization
changes.canonicalSummary: The original software synchronized calendars, contacts, mail settings, bookmarks, and media with a Mac or PC through iTunes.
changes.summary: Apple described computer synchronization as the setup and data-transfer model for the first iPhone generation.

citations.locator: Contacts, calendar, Safari bookmarks, and iTunes synchronization

changes.title: Camera and touch-based photo library
changes.canonicalSummary: The release integrated camera capture with a photo library supporting flick navigation, landscape viewing, wallpaper selection, and email sharing.
changes.summary: The software also synchronized photo collections from a computer and used device rotation to adapt presentation.

changes.title: Widescreen iPod and Cover Flow
changes.canonicalSummary: The built-in iPod experience combined touch navigation, landscape Cover Flow, and playback of synchronized music, podcasts, television, and movies.
changes.summary: Media controls changed with context, and rotating the device exposed album artwork browsing in Cover Flow.

changes.title: Rich HTML Mail
changes.canonicalSummary: Mail displayed formatted messages with images and supported common POP3 and IMAP services, including background retrieval.
changes.summary: Apple also promoted simplified setup for supported services and push delivery through Yahoo Mail.

changes.title: Mobile Safari
changes.canonicalSummary: Safari brought full-page web rendering, touch zoom, integrated search, and bookmark synchronization to the original iPhone.
changes.summary: Browsing operated over Wi-Fi or EDGE and presented desktop-layout pages through touch navigation.

changes.title: Google Maps
changes.canonicalSummary: The first release included maps, satellite imagery, traffic information, directions, and local search in a touch-oriented Maps application.
changes.summary: This initial implementation predated the automatic positioning enhancements that arrived in version 1.1.3.

changes.title: Sensor-aware interface behavior
changes.canonicalSummary: System software used the accelerometer, proximity sensor, and ambient-light sensor to rotate content, suppress accidental touches, and adjust brightness.
changes.summary: These behaviors were tied to the original iPhone hardware and should not be read as general support for later device families.

changes.title: Built-in YouTube application
changes.canonicalSummary: The shipping release included an Apple-designed YouTube client for browsing, searching, and streaming H.264 video over Wi-Fi or EDGE.
changes.summary: Apple announced the application specifically for the June 29 launch software and described the catalog as expanding during 2007.

citations.locator: iPhone YouTube application and June 29 availability

changes.title: Standards-based third-party web applications
changes.canonicalSummary: Apple’s initial third-party application path used browser-delivered software built with web standards instead of installable native packages.
changes.summary: Apple said web applications could invoke supported iPhone services such as calls, email, and map locations while remaining hosted and updated on the developer’s server.

citations.locator: Web 2.0 application model and supported services

events.summary: iPhone software 1.0.1 was the platform’s first public maintenance update, correcting five documented Safari, WebCore, and WebKit security weaknesses.

blocks.text: Apple’s first iPhone update focused on web-content security. It corrected cross-site access through redirected windows, unsafe regular-expression processing, injected XMLHttpRequest headers, deceptive internationalized domain names, and memory corruption while rendering framesets.

Apple distributed the package only through iTunes and identified the resulting version as 1.0.1. Its historical security index dates the release to July 31, 2007; no broader consumer feature list survives in Apple’s bulletin.

changes.title: Safari redirected-window access control
changes.canonicalSummary: Safari corrected a race condition that could let script on one page read or modify a redirected page outside its domain.
changes.summary: The correction tightened access to window properties during page updates and HTTP redirection.

changes.title: JavaScript regular-expression validation
changes.canonicalSummary: The update added validation around regular expressions to prevent heap buffer overflows in the JavaScript engine’s PCRE library.
changes.summary: Apple documented malicious web content as a route to a crash or arbitrary code execution.

changes.title: XMLHttpRequest header validation
changes.canonicalSummary: WebCore began validating serialized XMLHttpRequest header parameters to prevent cross-site request injection.
changes.summary: The weakness could be triggered by a malicious page crafting invalid HTTP request headers.

changes.title: Internationalized domain-name validation
changes.canonicalSummary: WebKit improved domain-name validity checks to reduce spoofing with visually similar Unicode characters.
changes.summary: Apple described the issue as a way for a malicious site to resemble a legitimate domain in Safari.

changes.title: Frameset rendering memory safety
changes.canonicalSummary: The release corrected an invalid type conversion in frameset rendering that could corrupt memory.
changes.summary: A maliciously constructed page could otherwise terminate the browser or execute arbitrary code.

changes.canonicalSummary: Version 1.1 brought Apple’s Multi-Touch mobile software environment to the first-generation iPod touch.

changes.title: iTunes Wi-Fi Music Store on iPod touch
changes.canonicalSummary: The initial iPod touch software let users browse, preview, purchase, and download music directly over Wi-Fi.
changes.summary: Purchased music synchronized back to the computer’s iTunes library on the next connection.

changes.title: Safari and YouTube over Wi-Fi
changes.canonicalSummary: iPod touch launched with Safari web browsing and a dedicated YouTube application using its built-in Wi-Fi connection.
changes.summary: Safari included integrated search and touch zoom, while YouTube exposed browsing and search for available video.

changes.title: Widescreen media and Cover Flow

changes.summary: Rotating the device changed supported media and browser views to landscape orientation.

changes.title: Orientation and ambient-light behavior
changes.canonicalSummary: iPod touch software used its accelerometer for landscape presentation and its ambient-light sensor for automatic display brightness.
changes.summary: The behavior applied to the first-generation iPod touch hardware and supported Photos, Safari, and Cover Flow presentation.

changes.title: iTunes Wi-Fi Music Store on iPhone
changes.canonicalSummary: The update added browsing, previewing, purchasing, and downloading iTunes music directly over Wi-Fi.
changes.summary: Songs obtained on the phone synchronized back to the computer’s iTunes library.

changes.title: Receiver and speakerphone volume
changes.canonicalSummary: The update increased the available volume for the phone receiver and speakerphone.
changes.summary: The surviving consumer list presents this as a general audio-level improvement rather than a hardware-specific repair.

changes.title: Home-button double-click shortcut
changes.canonicalSummary: A double press of the Home button could open phone favorites or music controls.
changes.summary: The shortcut provided quicker access to a user-selected high-frequency destination.

changes.title: Double-space punctuation shortcut
changes.canonicalSummary: The software keyboard gained an optional double-space shortcut that inserted a period followed by a space.
changes.summary: The feature shortened sentence punctuation on the touch keyboard and could be controlled from settings.

changes.title: Mail attachment rotation
changes.canonicalSummary: Mail attachments could be viewed in both portrait and landscape orientation.
changes.summary: The change extended orientation-aware viewing beyond the original attachment presentation.

changes.title: Reordering in Stocks and Weather
changes.canonicalSummary: Users could reorder tracked stocks and saved cities in their respective applications.
changes.summary: The update made the order of these user-maintained lists customizable.

changes.title: Apple Bluetooth Headset battery status
changes.canonicalSummary: The status bar could display the remaining battery level of Apple’s paired Bluetooth Headset.
changes.summary: The indicator was accessory-specific and should not be generalized to all Bluetooth headsets.

changes.title: Television output
changes.canonicalSummary: Version 1.1.1 added support for sending compatible iPhone media to an external television.
changes.summary: The preserved feature list identifies TV output but does not enumerate supported cables or media formats.

changes.title: International data-roaming control
changes.canonicalSummary: A setting was added to disable EDGE or GPRS data use while roaming internationally.
changes.summary: The control let travelers avoid unintended cellular-data use outside their home network.

changes.title: Passcode timing and alert-volume settings
changes.canonicalSummary: The update expanded passcode-lock timing choices and added control over alert volume.
changes.summary: These were user-facing configuration additions, separate from the security defects fixed in the same release.

changes.title: Bluetooth service-discovery validation
changes.canonicalSummary: The Bluetooth server added validation for crafted service-discovery packets that could crash software or execute code.
changes.summary: Apple limited the attack condition to an adversary within Bluetooth range while Bluetooth was enabled.

changes.title: Mail server identity warnings
changes.canonicalSummary: Mail began warning when an SSL mail server’s identity changed or could not be trusted.
changes.summary: The correction reduced credential and information exposure to an interceptor on an untrusted network.

changes.title: Telephone-link confirmation
changes.canonicalSummary: Mail and Safari tightened confirmation for telephone links so displayed and dialed numbers matched and calls were not placed unintentionally.
changes.summary: Apple documented separate Mail and Safari weaknesses and addressed both within the update.

changes.title: Safari cross-origin frame controls
changes.canonicalSummary: Safari strengthened cross-domain URL access, window-property controls, frame-source handling, and event association.
changes.summary: The grouped corrections covered URL disclosure and multiple cross-site scripting paths involving windows and frames.

changes.title: Immediate JavaScript preference enforcement
changes.canonicalSummary: Safari applied a changed JavaScript preference before loading subsequent pages instead of waiting for an application restart.
changes.summary: This prevented the interface from indicating that scripting was disabled while it remained active.

changes.title: HTTP and HTTPS frame isolation
changes.canonicalSummary: Safari restricted script access between insecure and secure frames served from the same domain.
changes.summary: The previous behavior could let HTTP content manipulate documents delivered over HTTPS.

changes.title: Automatic Maps positioning
changes.canonicalSummary: Maps could estimate the current location using nearby Wi-Fi access points and, on iPhone, cellular towers.
changes.summary: The estimated position could seed directions or nearby-place searches; Apple cautioned that availability and precision varied by location.

changes.title: Hybrid Maps view
changes.canonicalSummary: Maps gained a hybrid presentation that overlaid street and place labels on satellite imagery.
changes.summary: The view combined information from the existing map and satellite modes in one display.

changes.title: Web Clips and customizable Home screens
changes.canonicalSummary: Users could save website locations as Home-screen icons, reorder icons, and create as many as nine Home-screen pages.
changes.summary: A Web Clip could preserve the zoomed location within a page, turning frequently visited sites into launchable shortcuts.

changes.title: Group SMS conversations
changes.canonicalSummary: Messages could send one SMS to multiple recipients and retain the group history for later reuse.
changes.summary: Apple described the stored thread as a shortcut for sending another message to the same group.

changes.title: iTunes Movie Rentals playback
changes.canonicalSummary: The update played movie rentals transferred from a computer and added chapter navigation, alternate audio, and subtitle controls where available.
changes.summary: Movie-rental availability was region-limited at launch, while the playback controls depended on the transferred title’s content.

changes.title: Mail, Maps, Stocks, Weather, and Notes on iPod touch
changes.canonicalSummary: The iPod touch software upgrade added five Apple applications that had not shipped with early units.
changes.summary: Existing owners purchased the package, while newly manufactured iPod touch units included the applications.

changes.title: Rich Mail on iPod touch
changes.canonicalSummary: The iPod touch version of Mail supported formatted messages, background retrieval, and common POP3 and IMAP services.
changes.summary: Apple specifically documented setup for Gmail, Yahoo Mail, .Mac Mail, and other standards-based services.

changes.title: Foundation URL validation
changes.canonicalSummary: The system added validation for crafted URLs that could corrupt memory and terminate an application or execute code.
changes.summary: Apple’s archived bulletin lists the issue as affecting earlier iPhone and iPod touch software through version 1.1.2.

changes.title: Passcode Lock state validation
changes.canonicalSummary: The iPhone update tightened emergency-call state checks to prevent physical-access bypass of Passcode Lock.
changes.summary: The issue was iPhone-specific because the bypass involved emergency calling from the locked device.

changes.title: Safari frame-navigation policy
changes.canonicalSummary: Safari adopted stricter subframe navigation rules to prevent cross-site scripting and disclosure of sensitive information.
changes.summary: The weakness allowed one page to navigate subframes belonging to another page.
